courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset
md: Densification is driven by the *positional* gradient, not by the photometric error at a pixel directly. A region can look wrong yet not densify if its Gaussians are not being pushed around, which is one reason poorly observed regions stay blurry.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: One final score hides where the gain came from
md: An ablation turns one end-to-end number into a per-component account: what each stage adds, on the same queries and labels, under the same settings. Without it, you cannot tell which stage earns its latency.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
md: Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are where most real-world unsafe Rust lives, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
md: Do not hard-code 64 just because it is common. Query the line size (Drepper suggests compiling with `-DCLS=$(getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE)`), and if a binary must run everywhere, use the largest line size it may meet.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
md: The temperature turns a ranking of small cosine gaps into a confident probability. Its value decides how sharply the loss concentrates on hard negatives, which is why CLIP learns it and caps the logit scale at 100 for stability.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
md: Misconception: a column store is just a row store with one index per column. Abadi et al. tested exactly that (vertical partitioning and index-only plans in a commercial row store) and found it significantly slower, because the gains also come from the executor: compression-aware operators, late materialization and block-at-a-time processing.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: What -O0, -O2 and -O3 actually switch on
md: Misconception: "-O3 is always faster than -O2." -O3 makes code bigger and adds transforms that only pay off for some loops. Bigger code can cost instruction-cache misses. Measure both on your workload; -O2 is the common default for release builds.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: An atomic load followed by an atomic store is **not** an atomic read-modify-write. The fix here is `num.fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`, which makes L and S one indivisible step. Atomics remove data races; they do not remove race conditions in your logic.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: Use loom to search **schedules** of a tiny test exhaustively, and TSan to check **ordering** on real runs of the whole program. Neither proves correctness alone; together they cover far more than any number of stress runs.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: Bounded loads caps *load per server*, not *load per key*. If one key alone exceeds a server's capacity, forwarding spreads its requests across servers only when any server can answer for it, as with a cache that can fetch from the origin. A database shard that alone holds the data still needs the replication or splitting tools from the previous lesson.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
md: Choose the **variable** that is most likely to fail, and the **value** that is most likely to succeed. Every variable must be assigned eventually, so failing early on the hardest one costs nothing and prunes the most. But only one solution is needed, so values should keep the most options open.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: Misconception: a good standalone rewrite makes state unnecessary. To handle *drop the salary limit*, the rewrite must restate every surviving constraint as text, and the search engine must parse those constraints back into filters. That is two lossy conversions per turn, and a deleted constraint can come back if either one slips.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Ask when the readings are close in probability and a wrong guess is costly or hard to notice. Otherwise, guess the most literal reading, act on it, and make the interpretation visible.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: A clean CoT is not evidence of safety for tasks that do not need a CoT. Chen et al. and Korbak et al. both warn that malign reasoning can happen in activations, so a monitoring-only safety case fails there.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
md: Composition reshapes, divide tiles, slicing selects. local_tile picks a CTA's tile, local_partition or a TV layout picks a thread's share, and both are just layout algebra applied to the same tensor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: Pooling does not make stranding vanish. In the toy pooled design, host D still has 64 GB of local DRAM it cannot sell. Pooling helps because the *peaks* of different hosts rarely line up, so a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of per-host slack.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Domain weights are not a zero-sum allocation of quality. Because very easy and very noisy domains need few samples, and domains transfer to each other, a better mixture can lower loss on **every** domain at once, including the ones it shrinks.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus
md: Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Why distributed bugs refuse to reproduce
md: DST makes a run a pure function of (code, seed). Faults can then be as aggressive and random as you like, because any failure they provoke can be replayed exactly by re-running one seed.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
md: Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes
md: Choosing among the variants: DPO is the default for paired data with an SFT model. Use IPO-style or early-stopped training when labels are near-deterministic and you need to stay close to the reference; KTO when feedback is unpaired or imbalanced; ORPO or SimPO when a reference model is too costly. Whatever you choose, keep the chosen likelihood and output length under watch.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
md: Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
md: Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats
md: More levels are not free. The cascade API docs warn that adding levels is not always beneficial because of the overhead of merging attention results, and the paper notes real shared prefixes are often shorter than the long-prefix kernel benchmarks.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
md: A primed equation is not an assignment; an action is a true-or-false formula about a pair of states. If an action says nothing about a variable, the next value is unconstrained. TLC refuses such a spec: dropping `UNCHANGED tmp` from Write makes it stop with "Successor state is not completely specified by action Write".

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
md: Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
md: After fsync fails on buffered data, assume the dirty data is gone. Do not retry and continue: recover from a log you know is durable. That is why PostgreSQL's [data_sync_retry](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-error-handling.html) defaults to off, which turns such a failure into a PANIC and a WAL replay.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Use great-circle distance for the final answer. The sphere itself is a model: the Earth is slightly flattened, and a spherical model gives errors typically up to 0.3%. That is why PostGIS `geography` defaults to `use_spheroid = true`, and Elasticsearch `geo_distance` defaults to `distance_type: arc` (the faster `plane` is documented as inaccurate over long distances and near the poles).

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
md: The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
md: Fixed segments freeze their size at cudaMalloc time, so shapes that drift leave slivers. Expandable segments separate virtual addresses from physical memory (reserve once, map chunks as needed), so the segment grows contiguously instead.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: The headline result is GraphRAG versus vector RAG on global sensemaking questions: 72 to 83% comprehensiveness win rates on Podcast. Against map-reduce over raw text, the advantage is small; the bigger win there is token cost at query time.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: A higher IPC is not automatically better. A thread spinning on a lock retires instructions quickly, so it shows high IPC while making no logical progress. Judge IPC together with the instruction count and the run time.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: hugetlbfs: a reserved pool you map on purpose
md: A pool is memory you have given away. Those 3170 pages hold 6.2 GiB out of the page cache and away from every other process whether or not PostgreSQL is running. Over-sizing `nr_hugepages` is a common way to cause out-of-memory kills on a box that looks half empty.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Counting cache bytes: growing KV cache plus a fixed state
md: Hybrids do not help much at short context. At 1,024 tokens the cache formula gives only about 1.9x less memory for Nemotron-H-8B, and both the Jamba and NVIDIA papers report similar speed to Transformers at small context lengths. The gains grow with context and batch size.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: A robust change detector is: align (features, RANSAC, homography, optional ECC refinement), mask invalid warped borders, correct photometry using pixels that probably did not change, difference, threshold (Otsu when the histogram is two-humped), then open the mask with a kernel smaller than the smallest change you care about.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
md: Temperature does not change the argmax. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Do not evict a prefix's parent before its children. Because keys are chained, removing an early block makes every later block of that prefix unreachable, yet those stranded blocks still occupy space. SGLang's radix tree evicts leaves first for this reason, and Mooncake Store can evict a group of related objects (such as the separate K and V tensors of one entry) all or none.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: If clocks drift beyond the configured max offset, CockroachDB's docs warn that single-key linearizability between causally dependent transactions can be violated: a read can miss a write that finished before the read began (a stale read). HLC preserves the order it has seen, but it cannot fix a node whose clock is silently far behind. Run NTP or a similar time service and monitor the offset.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
md: Choose by what the extra slots carry. Fixed pause or filler embeddings add width within one pass. Coconut's fed-back hidden states and written CoT add serial depth across passes. Recurrent depth adds serial depth inside the network without any extra tokens.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
md: RankNet does not need graded labels, only a set of preferred pairs. Burges notes the pairs can even be inconsistent, for example from a confused judge who prefers U1 to U2, U2 to U3 and U3 to U1.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
md: Float descriptors (SIFT) are compared with L2 distance; binary descriptors (ORB) with Hamming distance. Binary descriptors trade some distinctiveness for much cheaper extraction, storage and comparison.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
md: Vocabulary trap. "Parsing accuracy" in the 2019 benchmark means grouping, not token-level correctness. Modern papers reserve **PA** for the stricter message-level metric where every static token *and* every parameter must be identified correctly, and use **GA** for grouping. A number quoted without its metric is worthless, so always ask: grouping or tokens, per message or per template?

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Multi-query is not a magic recall knob. In our toy no phrasing ever retrieves d8, so even the full union of all lists tops out at recall 0.8. Multi-query can only find documents that some phrasing ranks within the per-query depth.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: A reranker never finds anything. It can only reorder the list it receives. If stage 1 missed a document, no later stage, however large, can bring it back.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: Lossless means 'same output as greedy decoding with the next-token head'. With temperature sampling, accepting a draft needs the speculative sampling rule of Leviathan et al. to keep the output distribution exact; simply comparing argmax tokens would change it.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP = rotate into Shampoo's eigenbasis, run Adam there, rotate back. Refresh the rotation rarely; update Adam's statistics every step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
md: Before trusting muTransfer, run a coord check over a wide range of widths with a large learning rate. Flat curves after a few steps (apart from the output and attention logits at init) mean the parametrization is right.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: Choosing a lock: in application code use the standard mutex, which is already uncontended-fast and spin-then-sleep. Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, sharding) before tuning spin counts.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
md: When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: Remote memory is not slow like disk. It is the same DRAM, reached through one more hop, typically tens of percent slower per miss. The bigger danger is usually *bandwidth*: when all hot data sits on one node, one memory controller serves every socket while the others idle.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Balancing is not free. The kernel docs say the unmapping and extra faults cost overhead that is *ideally* offset by better locality, with no universal guarantee, and that it should be disabled when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes. Workloads that are already pinned and carefully placed are the natural candidates to turn it off.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: Duplicates are handled either after the fact by NMS, a hand-tuned greedy filter on IoU, or during training by one-to-one Hungarian matching, which teaches the model itself to emit one box per object.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Leases and timeouts alone do not fence. A paused process cannot notice that its lease expired while it was paused, so its next write happens anyway. Safety comes from the **storage rejecting** the stale writer: a conditional PUT on a slot the new writer already claimed.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
md: Never put an unbounded set in a label. The naming guide names the usual offenders: do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality, such as user IDs, email addresses, or other unbounded sets of values. Raw URLs with query strings, trace ids, error message strings and timestamps belong on the same list.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: Merging repeats happens **before** removing blanks. Doing it in the other order would turn b - o - o k into b o o k and then merge the o's into 'bok'.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Choosing PRIVATE for a dependency that appears in your public headers compiles fine for you and breaks for your users: their code includes your header, which includes D's header, but D's include directory never reached them. The error shows up in *their* build as a missing header.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
md: Small flake rates multiply across big suites: $P(\text{green}) = (1-p)^N$. Reruns buy back greens at the cost of hiding intermittent real failures. Fixing the flaky test is the only option without that cost.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
md: Fast does not mean shallow. Google's guide says reviewers must spend enough time that their approval really means the code meets the standard, and that if a change is too large to review quickly, the right response is to ask for it to be split into smaller changes, or at least send early comments on the overall design.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Common misconception: "I reviewed it, so I do not need to mention the tool." Under LLVM's policy review is required **and** substantial tool use should still be labelled. Under QEMU's policy, reviewing it does not help: AI-generated content is declined. The rules are per project.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: The manual's own warning: a bare `--force-with-lease` interacts very badly with anything that runs `git fetch` in the background, such as an IDE or a cron job. Each background fetch refreshes the expectation, so the lease can no longer tell "I saw this" from "something fetched this".

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
md: Compatibility is about combining code into one work. Permissive code flows into almost anything; copyleft code only flows into the same copyleft, and version clauses like 'only' and 'or later' decide which.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
md: Repetition fights noise; only experimental design fights bias. Same machine, same build flags, interleaved or balanced run order, and a second setup for surprising results.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Find the commit behind a change: log -S, -G and -L
md: Pick the tool by question. Who last touched this line: `git blame -w -M`. When did this text appear or disappear: `git log -S'text'`. Which commits touched lines matching a pattern: `git log -G'regex'`. How did this function evolve: `git log -L :func:file`. Then read the commit message and its pull request.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: Do not say "it is random". Tatham's advice is to try it several times, on another machine if you can, and report how often it fails and any pattern you notice, even a probabilistic one.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Misconception: "I will clean it up after review starts." Reviewers read what is there. Opening a non-draft PR with failing tests, debug code or an empty description tells them it is ready when it is not, and spends their first pass on things you could have caught.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Look for the widest top edges. Width is share of samples, y is ancestry, x order is alphabetical, and color is decoration.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
md: Undo log: old value durable before new value is written; commit point is invalidating the log. Redo log: new values durable in the log first; commit point is the commit mark. Either way, exactly one 8-byte-atomic event decides old versus new.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
md: Bottom-up is not free of crowd effects. The CNN pass is constant, but the number of candidate pairs per limb grows with the number of people, and the whole image goes through the network at one input size, so small, distant people cover only a few heatmap pixels, while top-down resizes every person to the same crop size.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Filtering during traversal is the right default for medium selectivity, but it has two failure modes at low $s$: a strict walk gets cut off (disconnection), and a walk-through degenerates into visiting about $k/s$ nodes. Both point to the same escape hatch: when matches are few, scan them directly.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K, Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
md: Misconception: "threads are cheap because the kernel treats them as lighter objects." On Linux a thread and a process are the same kind of task. A thread is cheaper to create because there is less to set up (no new address space or page tables), and switching between two threads of one process is cheaper because the address space stays loaded. Those savings come from sharing, not from a different kind of object.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
md: Raising code size cannot fix a too-small nprobe. The paper notes that increasing the code length is useless if w is not big enough, because neighbors outside the probed lists are never scored. Tune nprobe first, then code size.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
md: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and the log must reach stable storage *before* a server answers an RPC. If a server voted, crashed, and forgot its vote, it could vote again in the same term for a different candidate, and two leaders could be elected for one term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: Read the metrics as a grid. Low context recall: a **retrieval** problem. High context recall but low faithfulness: a **generation** problem. High faithfulness but wrong answer: the context itself was wrong or stale, an **index** problem.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Implicit feedback = preference (did it happen) x confidence (how sure we are). The confidence weights decide which events the factors must explain.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters
md: Map the object's **points** into plane millimeters first, then measure there. Never measure in pixels and convert with a scalar; the homography's division by w is where perspective gets removed.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: Synchronous does not mean "followers are always up to date for reads". With `synchronous_commit = on` the standby has *flushed* the record but may not have *replayed* it yet, so a query on that standby can still miss it. Only `remote_apply` waits until the change is visible on the standby, and the docs warn it causes much larger commit delays.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Goodhart measured: gold reward rises, then falls
md: Misconception: overoptimization is a fixed point you either cross or not. The curve is smooth. Gold reward usually *improves* first, which is why a rising training reward looks like success. You only see the turn if you evaluate with something other than the reward you train on.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted fairness in sched_ext can be three lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Everything else (CPU placement, preemption, latency boosts) is extra policy you choose to add.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: Colocation saves GPUs and keeps every GPU busy in a synchronous loop, but it forces phases to take turns and requires offloading. Separate pools only win if you also overlap rollout with training; on their own they just double the GPU count.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: An SAE is dictionary learning with a neural network: an encoder that picks a few latents, a decoder whose columns are the dictionary directions, and a loss that trades reconstruction against sparsity.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: The stack is not faster *memory*. Stack and heap bytes live in the same RAM behind the same caches. What is cheaper is *allocation*: one `sub` on `rsp` versus a search through allocator data structures. The top of the stack is also almost always hot in cache because it is reused constantly.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: A non-NULL return from `malloc` does not mean the memory exists. Under default overcommit a large allocation succeeds immediately, and the failure, if any, comes later as an OOM kill when the pages are first written, far from the line that allocated them.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Per-partition order is *write* order, not event-time order. If sensor A's readings were written late (e12 in our toy), they sit in the log after newer ones. Kafka removes the network chaos between bridge and processor, but it cannot undo disorder that happened before the write.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: Attention did not start with the Transformer. Additive attention over RNN states dates to Bahdanau et al. (2014). What was new in 2017 was using attention *alone*, with no recurrence or convolution.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
md: The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: $f'(x)$ answers: if I nudge $x$ by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does $f$ change? Positive means $f$ rises to the right, negative means it falls, zero means the tangent is flat.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
md: A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
md: An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Control flow is the program counter. Straight-line code advances it by the instruction length; `jmp`, conditional jumps, `call` and `ret` overwrite it. A C `for` loop compiles to a compare plus a conditional jump backwards.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index maps each term to a sorted list of the documents that contain it. A query reads only the postings of its own terms, so the work depends on how common those terms are, not on how big the whole collection is.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: Production inverted indexes are sorted, gap-encoded and block-compressed, and are written once into immutable segments that get merged, not edited in place. The ranking formula on top is a replaceable component.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Every malloc needs exactly one matching free, on every path out of the function. Missing it leaks memory; doing it twice, or touching the block afterwards, is undefined behavior that can corrupt the allocator's own bookkeeping.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|\cos\theta$. Its sign says whether two vectors point the same way (positive), at right angles (zero), or opposite (negative). Cosine similarity is the dot product with lengths divided out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: The loss you minimize is computed on the **training** data, but what you actually care about is performance on new data. Lessons 4 and 5 show how these two come apart.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout: train mode vs eval mode
md: BatchNorm and Dropout behave **differently in train and eval mode**. `model.train()` and `model.eval()` flip that switch for every such layer at once; forgetting either one is among the most common silent bugs in practice.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (branch speculation control) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
md: Total experience is the length of the union of role intervals, not the sum of their lengths. Sort by start, sweep, extend with max of the ends, and record gaps as you close blocks.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Surprise is not a separate score or probability the model predicts. It is the inner-loss gradient itself, the same quantity a TTT step already uses. Likewise $\eta_t$ here is momentum *inside the memory's inner loop*; it has nothing to do with the outer optimizer (AdamW) that trains the network.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
md: Every modern malloc fast path is the same idea as the 2001 magazine layer: a small, private stack of free objects per thread or CPU, refilled and drained in batches from a locked shared layer, with sizing policies to cap the memory that sits idle.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Fused softmax: one row per program, reductions on chip
md: Fusion in Triton is mostly a matter of keeping a tile in registers between operations. Load once, do every elementwise op and reduction on the block, store once.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: GenEval prompts are short and templated, and some models are trained mostly on long synthetic captions. Emu3's authors say exactly this and report rewriter numbers too. Before comparing two papers, check the rewriter, the CFG scale, and whether numbers were measured or copied from another paper.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
